## Saving and reusing scripts

The script that `--dry-run` prints is not a throwaway. It is a complete,
self-contained `ir` script. Redirect it to a file and you have a reproducible
artifact you can version, share, or run again later:

```{bash}
rush run --dry-run 'df |> dplyr::filter(body_mass_g > 5000)' penguins.csv > analysis.R
head -3 analysis.R
```

Run it with `ir run`. The `#|` frontmatter declares the script's dependencies,
so `ir` installs any missing packages and executes it. The saved script carries
its own dependencies and needs nothing but `ir` on the target machine:

```bash
ir run analysis.R
```

```{bash}
#| echo: false
Rscript analysis.R 2>/dev/null
```

The `#!/usr/bin/env -S ir run` shebang also makes the file directly executable
(`chmod +x analysis.R && ./analysis.R`). This is handy for tweaking: dump a
`rush` one-liner to a file, edit the generated R to do something `rush` does not
express directly, and run it later.

## Formatting with air

If the [air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/) formatter is on your `PATH`,
`rush` runs the `--dry-run` output through it, so the printed script is neatly
formatted and ready to save. This affects only what `--dry-run` shows; the
script that actually runs is never reformatted.

## Running without `ir`

By default `rush` runs each script with `ir`, which resolves the packages
declared in the frontmatter on the fly. If you would rather run against the
packages already installed in your library (for speed, to work offline, or in
an environment where dependencies are pinned), pass `--no-ir` (`-I`) and `rush`
runs the script with plain `Rscript` instead:

```{bash}
rush run --no-ir '6 * 7'
```

In this mode the `#|` frontmatter is left as inert comments and nothing is
installed, so every package the script needs must already be present. The
generated script itself is unchanged, so the same file still runs under `ir`
later.

```{bash}
#| include: false
rm -f analysis.R
```
